plan.question: How did one son overthrow his father and build a global power?

chapters.title: The Small State, The Big Bet
beats: A tiny nation in the Persian Gulf holds a secret: its leadership is about to split in two.
Regional giants, including Saudi Arabia and the UAE, watch from the sidelines as a son prepares to challenge his father.
The stakes are not just a throne, but the fate of a new foreign policy that will host rivals and mediate wars.
How did a single palace coup transform a quiet Gulf state into a global player?

chapters.title: The Father, The Son, The Loyalist
beats: Doha is the capital of Qatar, a land rich in gas but poor in land, making its rulers obsessed with security and influence.
Khalifa bin Hamad Al Thani, the Emir, wants stability; he has ruled since 1972 and sees his son as a risk.
Hamad bin Khalifa Al Thani, the Crown Prince, wants power; he has been given day-to-day control and dreams of independence.
Hamad bin Jassim, the Head of Police, is a loyalist to the old guard, positioning himself against the Crown Prince.
Fahad Al-Malki, the Deputy Head of Intelligence, stands with the Crown Prince, providing the secrets needed for a takeover.
Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, the Emirati Chief of Armed Forces, watches from Abu Dhabi, ready to support either side if the balance tips.

chapters.title: The Geneva Trap
beats: In 1992, Khalifa begins handing over the day-to-day running of Qatar to his son, a move that looks like trust but is actually a test.
Hamad uses this time to build his own cabinet and alliances, establishing the Qatar Investment Authority to prove his economic vision.
The Emir is away in Geneva, Switzerland, for a medical checkup, leaving his son in Doha with full control of the palace.
Hamad waits. He knows his father is distracted. The stage is set for a decisive move that will change the region's map.
chapters.hook: The Emir is gone. The son is waiting.

chapters.title: The Bloodless Takeover
beats: On 27 June 1995, Hamad bin Khalifa Al Thani seizes power in a bloodless palace coup.
He declares himself Emir of Qatar and Prime Minister, taking command of the defense and foreign affairs.
Khalifa bin Hamad Al Thani, upon hearing the news from Geneva, calls his son an "ignorant man."
The old Emir is offered refuge in the United Arab Emirates, but he remains a figurehead in exile, his authority stripped overnight.

chapters.title: The Counter-Coup
chapters.bridge: We go back to the immediate aftermath to see the first challenge to the new order.
beats: Hamad bin Jassim, the former Head of Police, leads a plot to overthrow Hamad bin Khalifa in February 1996.
Fahad Al-Malki, the Deputy Head of Intelligence, helps Qatari intelligence foil the attempt, known as Operation Abu Ali.
The plotters are captured. Hamad bin Jassim is tried and sentenced to life in prison for planning the coup.
85 defendants are convicted, showing the depth of the opposition to the new Emir's rule.

chapters.title: The Global Player
beats: Hamad bin Khalifa Al Thani launches Al Jazeera, a media empire that challenges regional voices, while increasing trade with Iran and Israel.
Qatar promotes its natural gas, reaching 77 million tonnes in annual LNG production, making it a global energy leader.
In 1999, Qatar holds its first elections for the advisory Central Municipal Council, allowing women to vote and stand as candidates.
Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, the Emirati Chief, watches as Qatar mediates the 2006 Lebanon War ceasefire and deploys 450 peacekeeping troops to the Djibouti-Eritrea border in 2010.
In 2005, the Emir donates $100 million to New Orleans after Hurricane Katrina, cementing Qatar's image as a generous, independent power.
